hints: Strain compares extension with the original length.
walkthrough: Let ΔL be the extension and L be the original length.
Strain is extension divided by original length: strain = ΔL / L.
It has no unit because both quantities are lengths.

ai_rubric.observable: Defines strain as extension divided by original length.

hints: Young modulus is stress divided by strain; calculate each quantity from the wire data.
Use the extension in metres and divide it by the original 4.0 m length before forming the ratio.
walkthrough: Young modulus is E = stress / strain.

ai_rubric.observable: Uses Young modulus as stress divided by strain.
Calculates stress from force and area and strain from extension divided by original length.
Obtains a Young modulus of 1.1 × 10¹¹ Pa.

hints: Up to the limit of proportionality, stress is proportional to strain.
Use the stress and strain calculated in part (b)(i) as the endpoint of the straight-line region.
walkthrough: Within the proportional region, Young modulus is constant, so stress is directly proportional to strain.
A directly proportional graph is a straight line through the origin.
From part (b)(i), the limiting strain is 3.5 × 10⁻⁴ and the limiting stress is 4.0 × 10⁷ Pa.
Draw the straight line from the origin to the plotted point with coordinates (3.5, 4.0) on the supplied scaled axes.

ai_rubric.observable: Draws a straight line through the graph origin.
Ends the line at the supplied-axis point (3.5, 4.0).

hints: For the same tensile force, compare the cross-sectional areas before comparing stresses.
Both wires are copper, so use how strain changes with stress when Young modulus is unchanged.
walkthrough: The second wire has a larger diameter and therefore a larger cross-sectional area.
With the same tensile force, stress = F / A is less in the second wire.
Both wires have the same Young modulus because they are the same material, and strain = stress / E.
The lower stress therefore gives lower strain, so tick less for both stress and strain.

ai_rubric.observable: Selects less for both the stress and strain of the larger-diameter second wire.
